_README: approach_variants for eleven MULTI-ROUTE alpine areas in the northern North Cascades plus three outliers filed in the same sweep (Raven Ridge in the Sawtooth, Snowking, and the Thunder Mountain / Slippery Slab Tower pair near Stevens Pass).

SCOPE WAS RE-QUERIED AND THE BRIEF'S COUNTS WERE STALE. Live counts by area_id: wa_jack_mountain 7 (brief said 5), wa_hozomeen_mountain 9 (brief said 2), and 2 each for the other nine areas - 34 routes in total. NOT ONE of the 34 had approach_variants, so every route in scope was a candidate.

27 routes written, 60 variants. 7 skipped, all recorded in _SKIPPED with the reason. Every skip is a row whose own approach column states that no approach is published, or that is empty, or that duplicates another row.

METHOD: re-homed from each row's own approach / waypoints / road columns, plus its siblings on the same peak, with web search used only to corroborate or to settle which of two sibling rows is right. Nothing was researched into existence: where a row says the approach is unpublished it was skipped rather than filled in. _confidence records which entries got outside corroboration ('corroborated'), which are purely re-homed ('re-homed'), and the one that rests on a row that contradicts itself ('thin', wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes).

NO hours, distMi or gainFt were written on any variant. Several of these rows carry published figures that conflict with their own columns or mix one-way and round-trip conventions, and averaging them would manufacture a number nobody published.
NO source names, author names, URLs or years appear in any name / season / notes / baseFinding / hazards field. Provenance is in _sources only.

CONTAMINATION REJECTED - Jack Mountain. The name is shared with peaks in Montana, Idaho and elsewhere. Resolved on area_id wa_jack_mountain and the peak coordinate 48.7728,-120.9564; every variant is anchored on access this peak actually has (Ross Lake's east shore, or the Canyon Creek trailhead on the highway). No out-of-state Jack Mountain material was used.

CONTAMINATION REJECTED - Bear Mountain. One of the commonest peak names in North America. Resolved on area_id wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack and coordinate 48.9306,-121.3412 in the Chilliwack Range; corroboration was accepted only where it named the Chilliwack approach and the north buttress.

CONTAMINATION REJECTED - Thunder Mountain. There are several in this state alone. The target area sits at 47.6689,-121.1263 in the Stevens Pass region, reached from the crest trail at Trap Pass - NOT the Thunder Creek / Thunder Mountain ground in the North Cascades near Diablo, and not the Thunder Mountain in the Sawtooth. Material about the North Cascades Thunder Creek was discarded.

CONTAMINATION REJECTED - Trapper Mountain (48.4318,-121.0184) is a different peak from Trappers Peak above Thornton Lakes, which is reached from an entirely different road. Search results for the latter were discarded.

CONTAMINATION REJECTED - Sinister Peak vs Dome Peak. Sinister stands just under a mile EAST of Dome on the same crest and shares Dome's entire approach, so descriptions of the two are constantly interleaved. Dome's own summit block material was excluded; the baseFinding for both Sinister routes carries the east-of-the-neighbour test explicitly, because this is the mistake the terrain invites.

BORDER ROUTES ARE GENUINE, NOT IMPORTS. The Depot Creek approach used for Mount Spickard and Southeast Mox Peak really does start on the Canadian side of the boundary and cross it on foot at a marker, and Hozomeen's road access really is from the Canadian side. These are recorded as the rows state them, with the passport and gate-status caveats, and no Canadian peak was pulled in as a Washington one. Every entry's area matches the live routes.area_id.

NAME TRAP INSIDE THIS BATCH: two unrelated 'Crater Lake / Crater Creek' systems appear here. Jack Mountain's Crater Lake lies on the Canyon Creek and Jackita Ridge trail system off the highway; Raven Ridge's Crater Lake lies on the Gold Creek and FR 4340 system near Twisp. They are on opposite sides of the range. Both are described by road and trail rather than by name alone, and Raven Ridge's variants carry an explicit warning about it.
A SECOND NAME TRAP: 'Little Jack' is a subsidiary summit on Jack Mountain's southwest ridge and the old trail to it is the approach for that route - it is not a separate peak with its own routes.

ROUTE IDS WERE NOT TRUSTED. Every entry was resolved by querying routes by area_id and asserting routes.area_id on the row itself. Four ids in this batch are name-shaped rather than peak-scoped (wa_east_ridge_2 is on Snowking, wa_direct_north_buttress is on Bear Mountain, wa_neve_glacier_west_ridge is on Snowfield, wa_the_devils_club is on Southeast Mox), and one id contradicts its own route name (wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib is the West Ridge) - see _DEFECTS.
READ-ONLY. Nothing was written to the database, nothing was committed, and no file in the repository was touched.

_SKIPPED.wa_jack_mountain_east_ridge: The row states in its own words that no single approach is documented as standard and that no source gives a turn-by-turn approach for this line; the base is described only as 'low on the glacier on the east side'. Two access options exist for that flank but neither is tied to a point where this ridge is gained, so any baseFinding would be constructed rather than re-homed.
_SKIPPED.wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge: The row states that no turn-by-turn approach is published and then borrows its terrain description wholesale from the Nohokomeen route's timber belt. Nothing fixes where the trail is left or where the ridge is gained, and the row itself calls the approach exploratory.
_SKIPPED.wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier: 69-character approach fragment ('North from May Creek; northeast face of mountain via glacier approach') and a probable duplicate of the Nohokomeen Glacier row, which starts at the same May Creek departure and climbs the same glaciated flank. Skipped as a duplicate rather than filled in; see _DEFECTS.
_SKIPPED.wa_hozomeen_mountain_north_peak_south_ri: Empty row - no approach, no grade, no description. This is the connecting ridge between the two Hozomeen summits, which is a notoriously rotten traverse that parties deliberately avoid; there is nothing in the row to re-home and inventing a base for it would be worse than leaving it blank.
_SKIPPED.wa_hozomeen_mountain_south_peak_north_ri: Empty row - the same connecting ridge seen from the other summit. Nothing to re-home.
_SKIPPED.wa_hozomeen_mountain_southwest_buttress: Empty row - no approach, no grade, no description. The peak's south-west and west basin ground is covered by the two populated routes on that side; nothing in this row identifies which buttress it is.
_SKIPPED.wa_thunder_mountain_north_face: The row states outright that the approach to the base of the north face specifically was not found, and that the only described access reaches the peak's SOUTH-EAST side from the upper lake. Writing a base-finding for the north face would mean deducing the base's position from aspect rather than re-homing it. The shared Trap Pass approach is captured on the sibling Slippery Slab Tower row.

_DEFECTS.wa_the_devils_club: The row's approach prose and its own waypoints describe approaches on OPPOSITE SIDES of the massif. The prose is the Ross Lake / Little Beaver / Perry Creek line to the East Face; four of the six waypoints (Depot Creek Falls, Ouzel Lake, Redoubt Glacier Camp, base of the East Face headwall) belong to the Depot Creek / Redoubt Glacier approach used by the peak's West Ridge route. The Depot Creek Falls waypoint here is at 49.01,-121.36 while the sibling row records the same feature at 48.9773,-121.2848 - roughly 9 km apart. A party navigating by the pins would walk the wrong approach for the route the prose describes.
_DEFECTS.wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib: Route id says 'se_rib' but the route name, the whole climbing description and the approach are the West Ridge. The id contradicts the row.
_DEFECTS.wa_direct_north_buttress: The approach column does not describe this route's approach. It routes the party off the maintained trail near the Copper Ridge junction and up Bear Mountain's WEST ridge to a camp near 4,600 ft, then describes the summit going via the west ridge and upper north ridge or the Northwest Ridge - i.e. the standard route, on the other side of the peak. The sibling North Buttress row carries the correct approach for both north-side lines (Bear Creek, then the 6,480 ft saddle on the north-west ridge). Variants here were re-homed from the sibling; the row's own text was not repeated.
_DEFECTS.wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes: The row contradicts itself about which drainage reaches Trapper Lake. The prose says to follow the valley trail to the Devore Creek trail junction and then push off-trail UP THE DEVORE CREEK DRAINAGE into the Trapper Lake basin; the row's own waypoint note at that junction says the route 'continues upstream on the Stehekin River Trail rather than turning up Devore Creek', and the Trapper Lake note says the lake is reached from the UPPER Stehekin River Trail. The recorded coordinates make the prose look like the wrong half: the junction is recorded at 48.3162,-120.6801 and the lake at 48.44,-121.0036, roughly 25 km apart up-valley, while the row records the lake at 7.5 miles from the trailhead. Reported, not fixed - the variant written here deliberately does not repeat the Devore Creek claim and tells the party to plan that section from current maps.
_DEFECTS.wa_jack_mountain_south_face vs wa_jack_m: Two rows on one peak disagree about the same trail. The South Face says Canyon Creek is crossed on a log-and-plank crossing and gives roughly 3,400 ft in 4 miles to the trail junction; the Southeast Ridge Direct says the Trail #738 bridge is DESTROYED and the creek must be forded, and gives about 62 switchbacks and 3,900 ft in 3.7 miles to Crater Lake. Their two Canyon Creek trailhead waypoints also differ by roughly half a kilometre. The crossing is the first obstacle of the trip and the two records give opposite advice about it.
_DEFECTS.wa_snowking_mountain_standard vs wa_east: The two Snowking rows describe the ridge junction differently and give OPPOSITE turns. The standard route says a cairned fork near 5,200 ft sends a fisherman's trail down toward Found Lake and to stay right and uphill; the East Ridge says there is an easy-to-miss junction at a saddle near Point 5116 and to go LEFT. They are most likely two different junctions on the same ridge, but nothing in either row says so, and a party reading both would have no way to tell. The variants written here keep each row's instruction with its own route and warn that the two are not the same fork.
_DEFECTS.wa_neve_glacier_west_ridge vs wa_snowfie: Probable duplicate. The 'Standard Route' row's own description gains the west ridge by the class 3 gully near 7,700 ft and finishes up it, which is what the 'Neve Glacier / West Ridge' row is named for. One row is far richer than the other and they share a trailhead, a camp, a col and a glacier crossing. Both were written for, since a party landing on either needs the approach, but they should be reviewed as one route split in two.
_DEFECTS.wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face: Two problems in one row. Its prose puts Trap Pass at about 5,800 ft while its own waypoint puts it at 5,050 ft. And FOUR waypoints share the identical coordinate 47.66888,-121.12634 - the base of the tower, the north-east face topout, the route start and the summit - so the row records the bottom and the top of a two-pitch face at the same point. The waypoint notes say these were corrected from an earlier error roughly 4.5 miles west; the correction appears to have collapsed them all onto the area coordinate.
_DEFECTS.wa_hozomeen_mountain_southeast_face: The row's prose and its waypoints describe different approaches. The prose is the Hozomeen Lake trail from the campground at the head of the lake, leaving it near the lake outlet and climbing the south basin; the waypoints are the Lightning Creek landing, Willow Lake, the 5,000 ft shoulder and the 6,200 ft saddle beneath the SOUTH-EAST BUTTRESS - which is the sibling route's approach. One waypoint note admits this in as many words and flags that the intended route may be the easier southwest line. Both approaches are written here as separate variants rather than merged, but the row needs deciding.
_DEFECTS.wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier: Two of the three waypoints have null lat and lng - the Silver Lake camp at 6,763 ft and the Custer-Spickard saddle at 7,380 ft. The saddle is where this route starts, so the one waypoint a party most needs is positionless. Also note the waypoint type is lowercase 'pass' where the rest of the catalog uses capitalised types.
_DEFECTS.wa_hozomeen_mountain (three empty rows): wa_hozomeen_mountain_north_peak_south_ridge, wa_hozomeen_mountain_south_peak_north_ridge and wa_hozomeen_mountain_southwest_buttress carry no approach, no grade, no pitches and no description at all. Two of them are the same connecting ridge between the peaks seen from either end, which is a rotten traverse parties avoid; whether they should exist as routes is worth deciding before anything is written into them.
_DEFECTS.wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier: 69-character approach and no other content, describing the same May Creek departure and the same glaciated flank as wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall. Likely a duplicate or a mis-split of the Nohokomeen route rather than a distinct line; the peak's documented glacier route is the Nohokomeen.

approach_variants.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
approach_variants.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
approach_variants.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb west to north-west, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TIMBER BELT IS THE NAVIGATION, THE GLACIER TOE IS THE ARRIVAL. Leaving May Creek you are looking for weaknesses, not a line: the cliff bands from about 3,200 ft up are passed on boot and game trails that thread left and right, so a section that forces you to climb rock means you have pushed into the band rather than around it. The reliable signal that you are through is underfoot rather than overhead - continuous snow starting somewhere near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and above that the timber gives out onto open ground.

THE CAMP IS A FLAT BENCH, NOT A VIEWPOINT. Just over 5,200 ft the ground levels into a flat bench directly below the toe of the ice. If you are on sloping heather with the ice still out of sight above you, keep going; if you are already on the ice you have walked past the bench.

THE HEADWALL IS ABOVE THE GLACIER, NOT AT ITS TOE. From the bench the glacier runs up in front of you at an easy angle for a long way before anything steepens. The route's steep ground is the wall at the head of that ice, directly beneath the summit. IF YOU ARE ROPING UP AND SWINGING TOOLS WITHIN MINUTES OF LEAVING CAMP, YOU ARE ON A SERAC OR A CREVASSE WALL LOW ON THE GLACIER, NOT ON THE HEADWALL. The headwall is only reached after the whole gentle bowl has been crossed and the ground ahead of you rears up as one continuous face rather than a series of rolls.

A CROSS-CHECK AT THE TOP OF THE ICE: the summit should be directly above the headwall, not off to one side. If the wall in front of you tops out on a shoulder with more mountain visible beyond it, you have drifted around the bowl.
hazards: steep brushy timber with cliff bands from about 3,200 ft, far worse to reverse than to ascend
crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, thinly bridged late in the season
sustained steep snow on the headwall itself, with a long runout onto the glacier below
rockfall and icefall off the wall once the sun reaches it
a two to four day commitment with no quick way off the mountain

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail
approach_variants.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
approach_variants.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LANDING THE FIRST TASK IS TO GET ONTO THE TRAIL AND FIND MAY CREEK - the East Bank Trail runs along this shore and the departure point is the creek, not a bearing. Once you leave the trail at May Creek every marker is identical to the walk-in variant: cliff bands from around 3,200 ft passed on game trails, continuous snow near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and the flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice.

THE ONE THING THE BOAT CHANGES IS YOUR MARGIN, NOT YOUR ROUTE. Parties dropped late in the day have started the timber belt in fading light, which is where the cliff bands become genuinely dangerous, because the passages through them are found by eye. If you cannot reach open ground above the bands in daylight, camp low rather than commit to the belt.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SAME: if the ground ahead of you steepens into rock rather than easing onto snow, you are in a cliff band and should traverse to find the boot track rather than force it.
hazards: fixed pickup times on a lake with no road out
the same steep brushy cliff-banded timber belt above the shore
arriving late enough that the timber belt is done in the dark
crevasses on the glacier above
no reliable communication once off the lake

approach_variants.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
approach_variants.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
approach_variants.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROAD SECTION IS NAVIGATION-FREE; THE APPROACH STILL STARTS AT MAY CREEK. Ride or ski the closed highway to the trailhead near milepost 138 and pick up the East Bank Trail there. The departure from the trail is the creek, as in summer.

WHAT CHANGES IS WHERE THE SNOW STARTS. In this window continuous snow is likely to begin well below the 4,800 to 5,000 ft line that summer parties describe, which means the cliff bands between roughly 3,200 ft and there are being crossed on snow rather than on game trails. A band that would be walked around in August may be a loaded slope in April. IF THE PASSAGE YOU WOULD NORMALLY TAKE THROUGH A BAND IS A SMOOTH, WIND-LOADED RAMP RATHER THAN A BOOT TRACK, TREAT IT AS AVALANCHE TERRAIN AND NOT AS A ROUTE.

The flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe may be buried and unrecognisable as a bench; in that case the arrival marker is the change of angle where the ground stops climbing and the ice begins running away ahead of you toward the wall.
hazards: avalanche terrain through the timber belt and on the glacier approach in early season
a long road section on bike or ski before the trip proper starts
short daylight and cold, with a committing position
cornices on the upper mountain
the road gate opening date moves year to year and can strand a plan

wa_jack_mountain_south_face._why: The south side is reached by a completely different trailhead from the Ross Lake routes, and the party then has to pick between two camps and two different lines off the same shoulder.

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Jerry Glacier crossing is reasonable and before fresh snow lands on the loose face
approach_variants.notes:
From the Canyon Creek Trailhead at about 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek and follow Trail #738 as it switchbacks hard through forest - three and a half to four thousand feet of climbing with no water on it, so fill up at the creek. Bear left at the Crater Lake trail junction and contour to the lake basin, then pick the trail back up above the lake for long, hot, exposed switchbacks with nothing to drink on them. Somewhere between 6,700 and 7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse to the gap between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak at about 7,200 ft. From that saddle the route goes downhill onto the Jerry Glacier: snow-covered and crevassed enough for a rope and crampons early, often patchy or bare late, when a slip runs further. Descend off the ice into the Jerry Lakes basin and fill water - it is the last of it before the face.

Check the Canyon Creek crossing before you commit: it has been described both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge gone, and it is the first obstacle of the trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FACE IS FOUND BY A SLUNG BOULDER AND A HIDDEN BREAK, NOT BY A BEARING. From the Jerry Lakes basin, traverse the heather shelf and go through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,000 to 7,200 ft. THIS SHOULDER IS THE DECISION POINT FOR THE WHOLE MOUNTAIN. For the South Face you now turn WEST and make a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, often moving in the shallow moat where old snow has pulled away from the rock.

THE POSITIVE MARKER IS A BOULDER WITH SLING MATERIAL ON IT, standing above the snow patches under the lower cliff band. The break in that band is a left-slanting ramp leading to a short class 4 step and then a hidden class 3 chimney, and IT STAYS INVISIBLE UNTIL YOU ARE ALMOST UNDERNEATH IT. Looking up from a distance and seeing no way through the band is the normal experience and is not evidence you are in the wrong place; looking up and seeing an obvious open gully is evidence that you are, because the break here is not obvious.

IF YOU ARE CLIMBING THE CREST OF THE RIDGE ITSELF RATHER THAN TRAVERSING BENEATH A FACE, YOU HAVE STAYED ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE AND ARE ON THE OTHER ROUTE. The South Face leaves the ridge at the shoulder and does not return to it until well above the cliff band, near 8,600 ft, where a band of scree beside a snow patch delivers you back onto the crest.

A CROSS-CHECK ABOVE THE BAND: 400 to 500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges linked by harder steps, then easier ground. Sustained hard climbing straight off the chimney means you have taken the wrong line through the band.
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the very start, which has washed out
long waterless switchbacks on both trail sections
crevasses and moats on the Jerry Glacier, worse as a bare-ice slip hazard late in the season
fire-damaged forest and unstable ground near Jerry Lakes
loose rock on the face where holds pull off freely - keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked
route-finding for the ramp and hidden chimney, which are hard to relocate on the descent

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows camp holds water later into the season than snow patches by the lakes
approach_variants.notes: The approach is identical as far as the Jerry Lakes basin and then forks on where you sleep. Camping at the lakes near 6,400 ft is the shorter day in and keeps water at the tent. Continuing over the notch just south of the lakes and dropping about six hundred feet into Crater Creek Basin puts camp in meadows near 6,000 ft north-west of Point 7,001 - a longer day in with a re-ascent at the end, but it starts summit day already on the right side of the notch and out of the wind.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER CAMP YOU USE, THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE SAME PLACE: THE LEVEL SHOULDER ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE NEAR 7,000 TO 7,200 FT. From the lakes you reach it by crossing the notch south of the lakes and climbing back out of Crater Creek Basin; from the meadows camp you climb straight to it.

THE SHOULDER IS RECOGNISED BY BEING LEVEL. The ridge relents here into a flat step before it rears up again, and the ground to the west opens into the scree traverse under the face. If you are still climbing steadily with no let-up, you are below it.

FROM THE SHOULDER THE SOUTH FACE GOES WEST AND DOWN-SLOPE OF THE CREST, ON SCREE AND DIRT, TOWARD SNOW PATCHES AND A SLUNG BOULDER UNDER A CONTINUOUS CLIFF BAND. If you find yourself scrambling directly up the crest above the shoulder you are on the Southeast Ridge line instead - a legitimate route, but not this one, and it has no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on it.
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of Crater Creek Basin if you camp low
no water above the lakes or the meadows
exposed camps with weather coming over the crest
loose ground on the traverse under the face

wa_jack_mountain_southeast_ridge_direct._why: It shares every step of the South Face approach and then deliberately refuses the traverse that route makes - so the whole difference is one decision made at one shoulder.
_sources: sibling row wa_jack_mountain_south_face for the shared approach detail

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, for dry rock on the crest and a crossable Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the South Face as far as camp. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead near 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek - reported both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge destroyed, so look at it before you commit - and grind up Trail #738's switchbacks through forest to the Crater Lake trail junction. Carry water from the creek; the hillside above has none. Continue past Crater Lake and up long exposed switchbacks, then leave the tread between about 6,700 and 7,200 ft and traverse to the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak near 7,200 ft. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, cross the saddle above Jerry Lakes, and camp at the lakes near 6,400 ft or in the Crater Creek meadows near 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS THE CREST, AND THE TEST IS THAT YOU NEVER LEAVE IT. From camp climb to the level step on the southeast ridge at about 7,000 to 7,200 ft. That step is the start: the ridge above it is the route, and everything you climb from there should have ground falling away on BOTH sides of you.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS HERE, BECAUSE THE WRONG TURN IS THE POPULAR ONE. From the same shoulder the South Face route turns WEST and makes a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, aiming for snow patches and a boulder with slings on it under a cliff band. IF YOU ARE WALKING SIDEWAYS ON SCREE WITH A WALL ABOVE YOU AND YOUR FEET IN A MOAT, YOU HAVE JOINED THE SOUTH FACE AND LEFT THIS ROUTE BEHIND. There is no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on the Direct.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THE SHAPE OF THE GROUND UNDER YOUR HANDS: the crest gives continuous scrambling with occasional steps rather than a traverse across a face, and the exposure is symmetrical. When the crest throws up a step you cannot scramble, the answer is a short pitch on the crest or a brief turn on its flank, not a traverse that takes you a rope length or more away from it.

A CROSS-CHECK HIGH ON THE ROUTE: near 8,600 ft the South Face rejoins the crest by way of a scree band beside a snow patch. If you are already on the crest well below that and stay on it, you and a South Face party will meet there having climbed two different mountains' worth of ground.
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the start
crevasses and steep neve on the Jerry Glacier both ways
loose blocks on the crest - the rock on this mountain pulls off freely
sustained exposure with rappels needed to reverse the steps
a long committing position with a multi-hour retreat to camp

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows hold running water later than the snow patches above the lakes
approach_variants.notes: The fork is only about where you sleep. The lakes near 6,400 ft are the shorter day in with water at the tent. Crossing the notch just south of the lakes and dropping into Crater Creek Basin to camp in the meadows near 6,000 ft costs a descent and a re-ascent but starts summit day on the correct side of the notch, directly under the shoulder where the ridge is gained.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BOTH CAMPS FEED THE SAME STARTING POINT - THE LEVEL STEP ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE BETWEEN ABOUT 7,000 AND 7,200 FT. From the lakes, cross the notch to the south and climb out of Crater Creek Basin to it; from the meadows, climb straight up to it.

RECOGNISE THE STEP BY THE GROUND GOING FLAT. The ridge eases into a level shoulder before rearing up again, and that flat is where the climbing starts. If the angle has not relented, you are still below it.

FROM THERE, STAY ON THE CREST. The moment the ground under you becomes a sidehill traverse on scree rather than a ridge with air on both sides, you have drifted onto the South Face's line beneath the cliff band. Turn back to the crest rather than continuing, because the two routes do not rejoin until near 8,600 ft.
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of the basin from the meadows camp
no water above the lakes or meadows
wind-exposed camps
loose ground on the climb back to the shoulder

wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge._why: It leaves the same trailhead as the Nohokomeen route and then takes a different branch at a junction two and a half miles in - so the two parties walk together and then part at a fork neither can see from the car.

approach_variants.name: The old Little Jack trail, taken as the rightmost branch of the junction on the East Bank Trail
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the ridge is clear of snow and while the meadow water sources still run
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Panther Creek and East Bank trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. Walk the East Bank Trail west for a little over two miles to a junction where several ways meet, and take the RIGHTMOST branch - this is the old Little Jack trail, cut a century ago to move pack animals up to the mountain's meadows, and it is neither signed nor maintained to the standard of the trail you have just left. It climbs steadily to Little Jack at about 6,745 ft, roughly four thousand eight hundred feet of gain from the junction. Water on the ridge is scarce and seasonal, so carry from low down rather than counting on the meadows.

This is the shortest line to the peak, and it is short in miles rather than in effort: the traverse from Little Jack to Jack is the part that takes the stamina.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE BRANCHES AT THE JUNCTION - THAT IS THE ONE NAVIGATION DECISION THE APPROACH ASKS OF YOU. Several ways meet a little over two miles along the East Bank Trail, and the Little Jack trail is the rightmost of them. A branch that keeps running level along the lake shore is the East Bank Trail continuing; a branch that starts climbing hard and does not stop is the one you want. IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING FLAT GROUND HALF AN HOUR PAST THE JUNCTION, YOU TOOK THE WRONG BRANCH.

LITTLE JACK IS A SUMMIT AND IT IS NOT YOUR SUMMIT. The trail tops out on an open, meadowy high point at about 6,745 ft that was grazed rather than climbed - broad, grassy, and unmistakably the end of a graded pack trail. Reaching it means the trail's work is done, and everything beyond is cross-country on the crest.

FROM LITTLE JACK, FOLLOW THE CREST NORTH TO THE NOTCH, THEN TRAVERSE ACROSS TO THE FOOT OF JACK'S SOUTHWEST RIDGE. The base you are looking for is where that traverse ends against the mountain proper and the ridge above you rises unbroken toward the summit. IF THE GROUND AHEAD OF YOU IS STILL ROLLING CREST WITH KNOLLS ON IT, YOU ARE BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS AND NOT YET AT THE BASE; if you can see glacier ice below you on the far side, you have crossed too far around the mountain and are looking at the northern flank.

THE OTHER USEFUL CHECK IS UNDERFOOT: the pack trail is graded and evenly cut, the crest beyond Little Jack is not. If you are still on constructed tread, you have not yet left Little Jack behind.
hazards: an unmaintained century-old pack trail that is easy to lose in the meadows
very little water once you leave the lake shore, and none reliable on the crest
a long exposed traverse between Little Jack and Jack with no bail-out
loose rock on Jack's ridge, and holds that pull
the descent reverses the whole traverse, so turnaround discipline matters more than usual here

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre._why: Two countries offer approaches to the same wall and they are not interchangeable; and once at camp the route starts by going DOWN, which is where parties get it wrong.
_sources: web corroboration that the regular line takes the glacier on the buttress's climber's-left side

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS BY LOSING HEIGHT, AND THAT IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW AT CAMP. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS UPWARD FROM THE SADDLE TOWARD ROCK IS THE WRONG ONE.

IDENTIFY THE SADDLE FIRST: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

AT THE ICE, THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE BUTTRESS YOU GO UP. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS ITSELF, WHERE THE ROCK MEETS THE ICE ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE, IS THE START OF THE DIRECT AND NOT OF THIS ROUTE. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

WATCH THE JOIN BETWEEN SNOW AND ROCK. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A CROSS-CHECK ONCE COMMITTED: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.
hazards: a river crossing that depends on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread
loose south-facing traverse slopes below the divide points
rockfall and icefall out of the shrinking glacier in the couloir
a moat between neve and slab that worsens through the season
a position days from any road, on either side of the border

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only with the paperwork in hand
approach_variants.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It costs a legal border crossing, so passports and a plan for entering the country on foot are not optional, and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH VARIANT CHANGES ONLY HOW YOU ARRIVE AT THE 6,480 FT SADDLE. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by DROPPING off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

THE SAME TWO TESTS APPLY AT THE ICE. Go up the snow on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE MARKER: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with the documents and permissions that implies
unmaintained and heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
the same loose divide traverse and the same glacier remnant beneath the buttress
a rescue that may involve two countries

wa_direct_north_buttress._why: It shares a camp and a walk-in with the regular North Buttress and then starts somewhere else entirely - on the opposite side of the same piece of ice.
_sources: web corroboration that the toe of the direct buttress lies on the right of the glacier while the regular line continues up the glacier on the buttress's climber's left

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-pulled cable car and a serious ford without it, then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since fire came through, so confirm rather than assume.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRECT STARTS AT THE VERY BOTTOM OF THE ROCK, AND THAT IS WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE ROUTE IT SHARES A CAMP WITH. From the saddle you first go DOWN: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS LIES ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THAT ICE, WHERE THE ROCK RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW. THAT JUNCTION IS THE START. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND IT IS THE COMMON MISTAKE: THE REGULAR NORTH BUTTRESS WALKS PAST THIS TOE AND CONTINUES UP THE GLACIER ON THE BUTTRESS'S CLIMBER'S-LEFT SIDE, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING ON SNOW WITH THE BUTTRESS RISING TO YOUR RIGHT, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE DIRECT AND ARE HEADING FOR THE REGULAR START. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A SECOND CHECK IS HOW SOON IT GETS HARD. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

WATCH THE MOAT AT THE JUNCTION. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.
hazards: a river crossing dependent on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber, slide alder, and a loose divide traverse
rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir
a deep moat at the toe of the buttress late in the season
sustained hard climbing days from the nearest road, with a descent onto the other side of the peak

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.season: Same window, with passports
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, at the price of a legal border crossing on foot and an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL DIFFERS, THE START DOES NOT. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

TIE IN AT THE TOE OF THE ROCK ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE ICE, WHERE THE BUTTRESS RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW AND THERE IS NO MORE SNOW ABOVE YOU. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
overgrown unmaintained tread
the same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall beneath the buttress
a cross-border rescue picture

wa_hozomeen_mountain_southeast_face._why: Hozomeen has no road on the United States side, so the first decision is boat, gated border road, or a long trail from a different landing entirely - and the three put you on opposite sides of the massif.
_sources: sibling rows on the same peak for the alternate landings

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the campground at the head of the lake
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the brush is passable and the upper gullies have melted out
approach_variants.notes:
There is no public road to this end of the lake from the south. Drive to the trailhead near milepost 134, walk down to the resort, and take its water taxi north to the campground and ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,650 ft. Everything below is measured from there.

From the campground pick up the maintained lake-side trail, which climbs gently through open lush forest toward Hozomeen Lake. Reports differ on how far along it you should stay - anywhere from a mile and a half to four miles depending on where the party cut off - so budget for the longer figure. Leave the tread around 2,400 ft near the lake's outlet and start up cross-country, following the drainage east into the basin under the peak's south side. There is a genuinely bad brush section here: devil's club right at the creek crossing, and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft that reduces travel to a crawl. Fill water at the creek crossing or again in the basin near 5,000 ft, because everything above is dry.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LADDER OF LANDMARKS ABOVE THE BASIN IS WHAT FIXES YOUR POSITION, AND THEY COME IN ORDER. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones - IF YOUR GULLY HAS NO CHOCKSTONE BOTTLENECK IN IT, YOU ARE IN THE WRONG DRAINAGE and should traverse rather than climb. Above the chockstones the ground turns to tedious red scree and heather. The next confirmation is a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, passed rather than climbed. Above it the angle steepens to a broad saddle and basin near 6,800 ft with small flat tent-sized sites - the standard high camp, good for one or two tents and no more.

FROM CAMP THE BASE OF THE ROUTE IS ANOTHER THOUSAND FEET OR SO ABOVE, GAINED ON SLABS AND CONNECTING GULLIES. You are looking for the point where the slabs run out against the face and the ridge proper takes over.

CHECK WHICH SUMMIT IS ABOVE YOU. This route is on the SOUTH peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. If the tower above you is the higher, broader one and the other summit lies to the SOUTH of you, you have drifted north into the wrong cirque and are under the north peak.

AND CHECK THAT YOU LEFT THE TRAIL AT ALL. The maintained tread is graded and obvious; the moment you are on it with easy walking under your feet, you are not on the approach any more. The departure is at a creek, at a lake outlet, not at a sign.
hazards: a boat schedule that fixes both ends of the trip on a lake with no road out
devil's club at the creek crossing and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft
no water above the basin near 5,000 ft
a boulder-choked gully with chockstones to negotiate under a pack
loose, friable rock on the upper mountain
a tiny high camp that will not take a large party

approach_variants.name: By road from the north to the ranger station, subject to the border gate
approach_variants.season: July through September, and only if the boundary is open
approach_variants.notes:
The campground and ranger station at the head of the lake can also be reached by driving a long gravel road south from the north side of the international boundary. That crossing has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic, so this variant may simply not exist in the season you are planning for - confirm the gate's status before building a trip on it, because there is no way to discover it is shut except by arriving.

If it is open, the walk from the campground is identical to the boat variant: the maintained lake-side trail toward Hozomeen Lake, then off-trail at the outlet near 2,400 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL CHANGES, THE APPROACH DOES NOT. From the campground at about 1,650 ft the sequence is the same: maintained trail to the vicinity of Hozomeen Lake's outlet near 2,400 ft, then cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east into the south basin.

THE MARKERS ARE THE SAME LADDER, IN THE SAME ORDER: a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones near 5,000 ft, red scree and heather above it, a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, and then a broad saddle and basin at about 6,800 ft with a few small flat tent sites. A drainage with no chockstone bottleneck is the wrong drainage.

THE SUMMIT TEST STILL APPLIES. This route is on the SOUTH peak, the lower of the two. If the higher, broader summit is directly above you and the other one lies south, you are under the north peak instead.
hazards: a border gate that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services at the end
the same devil's club, deadfall and dry upper slopes
loose rock and a small high camp

approach_variants.name: From the Lightning Creek landing on the lake's east shore, past Willow Lake
approach_variants.season: July through September
approach_variants.notes: A boat landing further down the east shore of the lake gives onto the east-bank trail system, which runs north past Willow Lake. Parties have used this to reach the south and south-east sides of the massif on foot rather than starting from the campground at the head of the lake. It is the longer walk of the two boat options and it approaches the peak from the south-east rather than from the west, so it suits parties heading for the south-east side of the south peak more than it suits the standard line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEPARTURE FROM THE TRAIL IS JUST BEYOND WILLOW LAKE, AND THE LAKE IS THE MARKER. It is the last reliable water; everything above is dry until the basin, so this is where you fill.

FROM THERE THE GROUND IS THE TEST RATHER THAN ANY TREAD: timber and avalanche debris first, then a ravine to cross, then steep dirt and brush climbing to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Reaching MEADOWS near 5,000 ft is the sign the worst of the brush is behind you.

ABOVE THE MEADOWS THE CLIFF BANDS ARE BYPASSED, NOT CLIMBED. If you are forced onto rock that wants a rope, traverse and look for the way round rather than committing to it - the way through here is a walking line, not a climbing one.

THE ARRIVAL IS A SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,200 FT DIRECTLY BENEATH THE BUTTRESS on the peak's south-east side, with no water on it. IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED SOMEWHERE WITH RUNNING WATER, YOU ARE NOT THERE YET. From that saddle the standard south-east face and the south-east buttress lines are both above you, so identify which feature you are under before starting up.
hazards: a much longer walk than the head-of-lake landing
timber, avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water between Willow Lake and the basin
cliff bands that must be bypassed in poor visibility

wa_hozomeen_mountain_south_peak_southwes._why: It leaves the same trail as the standard south-side line but turns into a different basin, and the row that describes it is brief enough that a party would otherwise be guessing.
_sources: sibling row wa_hozomeen_mountain_southeast_face for the shared trail and creek crossing

approach_variants.name: The lake-side trail from the campground, leaving it at the Hozomeen Lake outlet for the west basin
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the west basin has melted out
approach_variants.notes:
From the campground and trailhead at roughly 1,650 to 1,720 ft, a maintained trail runs toward Hozomeen Lake. Climbers leave it near the lake's outlet, cross Hozomeen Creek, and push east into the peak's west basin through heavy deadfall and devil's club - the brush here is the defining feature of the approach rather than an incidental one. The basin gives onto a rib and gully system that leads to a high camp or bivouac around 4,900 to 5,000 ft, and above that to a saddle reported near 6,800 ft below the final pitches.

Getting to the campground itself is the trip's first problem: either the resort water taxi up the lake, or the long gravel road down from the north side of the boundary, which has been closed to vehicles and walkers alike. Settle that before anything else.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WEST BASIN IS ENTERED AT A CREEK CROSSING, NOT AT A VIEWPOINT. Leave the maintained trail near the outlet of Hozomeen Lake and cross Hozomeen Creek; if you are still on graded tread you have not left yet, and if you have not crossed water you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

THE BASIN ITSELF IS RECOGNISED BY WHAT STOPS: the deadfall and devil's club that define the lower push give out as the ground steepens into a rib and gully system. THAT RIB IS THE LINE - a gully with no rib beside it to escape onto is not the one, because the way up here uses both.

THE FIRST FIXED POINT IS THE BIVOUAC GROUND AT ABOUT 4,900 TO 5,000 FT, where the rib eases enough to lie down on. Above it the system continues to a saddle at roughly 6,800 ft, and that saddle is the base: the final pitches start from it.

CHECK THE PEAK ABOVE YOU BEFORE COMMITTING. This is a route on the SOUTH peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. IF THE SUMMIT ABOVE YOU IS THE HIGHER, BROADER ONE AND THE OTHER LIES TO THE SOUTH, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR NORTH AND ARE IN THE NORTH PEAK'S GROUND. The connecting ridge between the two is notoriously rotten and is not a way to correct the error from above; go back down and around.
hazards: heavy deadfall and devil's club through the whole lower basin
a creek crossing to enter the basin
loose rock on the rib and gully system
an exposed high bivouac with limited flat ground
reaching the trailhead at all, which depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate

wa_hozomeen_mountain_south_peak_southeas._why: It is the one line on the massif approached from the lake's east shore rather than its head, so a party using the usual campground start is on the wrong side of the mountain from the outset.
_sources: route row approach and waypoint columns (re-homed)

approach_variants.name: Lightning Creek landing and the east-bank trail past Willow Lake
approach_variants.season: July through September
approach_variants.notes: Take the boat landing on the lake's east shore rather than continuing to the head of the lake, and pick up the east-bank trail there. Follow it north past Willow Lake, which is the last reliable water. Beyond the lake the trail is left behind and the travel becomes timber and avalanche debris, a ravine to cross, and then steep dirt and brush up to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Meadows near 5,000 ft mark the end of the worst of it. From the meadows the cliff bands are bypassed on their west side rather than forced, and the ground leads to a saddle at about 6,200 ft directly beneath the buttress. The first ascent party bivouacked there, roughly six hours from the landing, and there is no water on it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WILLOW LAKE IS THE POINT OF DEPARTURE AND THE LAST WATER - FILL THERE, BECAUSE NOTHING ABOVE RUNS. Leave the trail just beyond it and turn east.

THE SEQUENCE UNDERFOOT IS THE NAVIGATION: timber and avalanche debris, then A RAVINE THAT MUST BE CROSSED, then steep dirt and brush. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A RAVINE, YOU HAVE NOT YET COMMITTED TO THE RIGHT LINE. Above the brush the timber opens onto a broad shoulder and then meadows near 5,000 ft.

THE CLIFF BANDS ARE PASSED ON THEIR WEST SIDE. Anything that wants a rope on this section means you have run into the band rather than round it.

THE BASE IS A DRY SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,200 FT WITH THE BUTTRESS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. Two confirmations: the buttress above you is DIVIDED rather than a single clean rib, and the way onto it starts with a steep chimney low down - a face with no chimney at its foot is not this buttress. If your saddle has running water on it you are somewhere else, because this one has none.

AND CHECK THE PEAK: this is the SOUTH peak, the lower of the two summits. The higher, broader summit should be to the north of you, not above you.
hazards: the longest walk-in of the massif's options
avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water above Willow Lake, and a dry bivouac at the saddle
friable rock on the buttress with scarce protection
a loose upper gully above the crux chimney

wa_hozomeen_mountain_north_peak_north_ro._why: The north peak is reached from the campground by a west-flank bushwhack that shares nothing with the south peak's basin, and the party has to know which side of the massif it is committing to before leaving the water.
_sources: sibling row wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress for the alternative from the north

approach_variants.name: The short loop trail at the ranger station, then the west flank to the heather knoll
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the west flank is clear of snow
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,600 ft and pick up the short interpretive loop that begins there. Leave it eastward, cross Howlett Creek, and climb cross-country through moderately open forest on the mountain's western flank. There is no trail above the loop.

The forest goes reasonably on the way up and badly on the way down: parties consistently report dense brush and jackstraw deadfall as the time sink of the descent rather than of the ascent, so mark your line as you climb rather than trusting to memory.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL IS A CHANGE OF VEGETATION, NOT A CHANGE OF ANGLE. Climb the west flank until the timber gives out onto a HEATHERY KNOLL at about 5,900 ft. That knoll is where the north ridge is gained and where the route starts. IF YOU ARE STILL IN TIMBER, OR IN JACKSTRAW DEADFALL AND BRUSH, YOU ARE BELOW IT - the knoll is open ground and unmistakable when you reach it.

THE RIDGE ABOVE THE KNOLL IS THE ROUTE, AND IT SHOULD HAVE AIR ON BOTH SIDES. If you are climbing a face with the crest still above you and to one side, you have gained the flank rather than the ridge and should traverse to the crest before continuing.

CHECK WHICH SUMMIT YOU ARE UNDER. This is the NORTH peak, the higher and broader of the two main summits. THE OTHER SUMMIT SHOULD BE TO THE SOUTH OF YOU. If the higher ground lies north and you are looking up at a tower with a rotten connecting ridge running toward it, you are on the south peak's flank instead, and the ridge between them is not a way to correct that - it is a notoriously rotten traverse that parties deliberately avoid.

A CROSS-CHECK ON THE DESCENT: you must find the knoll again to get back into the correct drainage. From above, the flank is uniform timber in every direction, and the drainage you came up is only identifiable from the knoll's position. Fix it before you leave it.
hazards: no trail above the interpretive loop, and a descent through jackstraw deadfall and brush that is far slower than the ascent
a creek crossing at Howlett Creek
route-finding on a uniform forested flank with no landmarks below the knoll
steep snowfields low on the route in early season
loose class 3 and 4 rock on the ridge above
reaching the ranger station at all depends on a boat or on a closed border gate

wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress._why: Two ways reach the same north cirque and one of them saves miles and costs hours - and both start on the far side of an international boundary whose gate may be shut.

approach_variants.name: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
approach_variants.season: July through September; the gravel road governs the season at its own end
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this peak from the south. From the highway on the north side of the boundary, follow the valley road south on gravel through the provincial park to the trailhead - a slow drive of well over an hour. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning: the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic.

From the trailhead, climb roughly four thousand feet on trail to the ridge junction, then turn south along the ridge over rolling ground to a camp near the boundary high point at about 6,345 ft. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below the ridge, because there is none again until you are well south of the boundary.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CAMP THE ROUTE STARTS BY LOSING HEIGHT - ABOUT 545 FT DOWN TO THE 5,800 FT SADDLE AT THE HEAD OF THE NORTH CIRQUE. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS FROM THE CAMP IS THE WRONG WAY. The saddle is the low point at the head of a bowl, with the cirque falling away in front of you and the buttress rising on its far side.

RECOGNISE THE CIRQUE BY ITS SHAPE: it is an enclosed bowl beneath the north side of the peak, not an open flank. If the ground ahead of you drops away into a valley rather than into a bowl with walls around it, you have gone off the ridge too early or too late.

THE BUTTRESS IS ON THE NORTH-EAST SIDE, so from the saddle it should stand between you and the sun in the middle of the day rather than in it. A wall you approach in full afternoon sun is on the wrong aspect.

CHECK THE PEAK: this is the NORTH summit, the higher and broader of the two. The other main summit should lie to the south, connected by a rotten ridge that is not a usable link between them.

WATER IS THE OTHER FIXED POINT. The last of it is the creeks in the forest below the ridge junction, well before camp. If you have passed those without filling, the correct move is to go back for water rather than to press on to a dry camp above a dry cirque.
hazards: a boundary crossing that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services
no water south of the creeks below the ridge junction
an exposed ridge camp
a 545 ft descent from camp that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
loose rock on the buttress

approach_variants.name: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station
approach_variants.season: July through September, and slower than its distance suggests
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter start leaves from the ranger station at the head of the lake, follows the short interpretive loop, and then bushwhacks east up the overgrown boundary swath, past a swamp, gaining about three thousand feet to a col near 6,300 ft where it joins the ridge. It saves miles and costs hours - the swath is overgrown rather than cleared, and the ground is steep and brushy. Reaching the ranger station itself means either the water taxi up the lake or the gated road from the north.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SWATH IS THE HANDRAIL - IT IS A CLEARED LINE THROUGH FOREST THAT RUNS EAST, AND IF YOU ARE NOT ON IT YOU ARE NOT ON THE APPROACH. It is overgrown, so it looks like brush rather than like a corridor from inside it; the tell is that it is straight, and it does not wander with the terrain the way a game trail does.

A SWAMP IS PASSED LOW DOWN. Reaching it confirms the line; never reaching it means you have drifted off the swath into ordinary forest.

THE JOIN IS A COL NEAR 6,300 FT, roughly three thousand feet above the start, where the swath's climbing ends against the ridge. From there the route is the same as the long approach: work along to the saddle at the head of the north cirque near 5,800 ft, WHICH MEANS LOSING HEIGHT AGAIN, and the buttress stands on the far side of the bowl.

IF YOU ARRIVE ON A RIDGE AND THE GROUND BEYOND IS AN OPEN VALLEY RATHER THAN AN ENCLOSED BOWL, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG COL. The cirque is walled; the valley is not.
hazards: an overgrown boundary swath that is steep, brushy and slow
a swamp low on the line
three thousand feet of unrelenting bushwhacking with no tread
no water on the upper half
reaching the ranger station depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate

wa_hozomeen_mountain_west_face._why: The approach from camp to the foot of this wall is a half-day objective of its own and it goes DOWN a loose gully first - the row says so, and nothing else on the peak does.

approach_variants.name: Ridge camp north of the peak, then the traverse down and across to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.season: Mid-summer, and the base approach should be done in daylight
approach_variants.notes:
Two stages, and the second is what stops people. The first is a long day of eleven miles and more under heavy loads from the road on the north side of the boundary to a camp just north of the peak - the same ridge and boundary-swath ground the north-side routes use. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning any of it.

The second stage is the approach from that camp to the base of the wall, which the first ascent party found tedious and painstaking and which took them four and a half hours. Budget it as a half-day objective in its own right and do it in daylight; there is no version of this traverse that goes well in the dark.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST MOVE OUT OF CAMP IS A DOWNCLIMB, NOT A CLIMB. A loose third-class gully drops from the ridge camp toward the west side, and the party who first did it called it dangerous but the lesser of two evils - meaning the alternatives were worse, not that the gully is good. IF YOU ARE GAINING HEIGHT ON LEAVING CAMP, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE RIDGE.

BELOW THE GULLY THE TRAVERSE IS THE ROUTE-FINDING: SEVERAL PRECIPITOUS ROCKY RIBS, CROSSED ONE AFTER ANOTHER, ON STEEP UNSTABLE GROUND. Counting ribs is the only progress measure you have. A traverse that stays on one continuous slope without crossing ribs is not this one - it means you have dropped too far and are below the line, on ground that leads away from the wall rather than across to it.

THE ARRIVAL IS A LAUNCH POINT BENEATH THE WALL, with the face rising directly above and no further traversing to do. THE WALL FACES WEST, so it takes the afternoon sun and stands in shadow in the morning - if the face above you is lit at dawn, you are on the wrong aspect and have crossed too far around the peak.

TIMING IS PART OF THE NAVIGATION HERE. Four and a half hours from camp to the base means a party that leaves at first light arrives late morning; a party that leaves late arrives with the wall in full sun and the loose ground behind them to reverse in the dark.
hazards: a loose third-class gully downclimbed at the start of the day, and re-climbed at the end of it
several precipitous rock ribs on steep unstable ground
a base approach long enough to be its own objective
a west aspect that takes afternoon sun and afternoon rockfall
a boundary gate that has been closed to vehicles and walkers
a remote position with a heavy carry to camp

wa_mount_spickard_southwest._why: Two approaches from two different countries reach two different camps on opposite sides of the peak, and the point where you leave the drainage is before a saddle rather than at it.
_sources: sibling row wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier for the lake-side alternative

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CRITICAL INSTRUCTION IS THAT YOU LEAVE THE DRAINAGE BEFORE THE PASS, NOT AT IT. From camp, ascend the broad talus couloir and stream drainage north to north-east toward the saddle at roughly 7,200 ft - but WELL BEFORE reaching that saddle, cut RIGHT around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather and moraine basins.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXACT AND EASY TO USE: IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED AT THE SADDLE AND ARE LOOKING DOWN INTO THE CIRQUE ON THE FAR SIDE, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR. Go back down and find the buttress toe.

THE BUTTRESS TOE IS THE FEATURE - a steep rock nose that the couloir runs past on its left. Turning its foot puts you into open heather and moraine, which is different ground from the couloir you have been climbing, and that change underfoot is the confirmation.

THE BASE IS THE TOE OF THE SOUTH-WEST GLACIER, reached by traversing those basins. Rope up and put crampons on there rather than part-way across. THE LINE UP THE ICE IS ITS CLIMBER'S-RIGHT MARGIN, which holds hard snow and ice at thirty to forty degrees and relatively few crevasses; about half-way up, one poor-looking crevasse has to be crossed on a marginal bridge, so probe it and expect it to be worse late in the season.

CONFIRM AT THE TOP OF THE ICE: a short steep loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on a low col on the south-west ridge, above the cirque. That col is where the summit scramble starts. If the ice runs you out onto a broad snow shoulder with no gully and no col, you have taken the glacier's centre or its left side instead of its right margin.
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with a register at the obelisk
a road that washes out and lengthens the walk without warning
wet slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls, with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
crevasses on the south-west glacier and one marginal snow bridge on the standard line
a short steep loose gully at the head of the glacier
thirty-five to forty degree snow near the summit ridge

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE OLD CABIN AT ABOUT 2,900 FT IS THE PROOF YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE CREEK. The trail climbs the NORTH side; if you have not passed a cabin by the time the trail gives out, you are on the wrong bank and should cross before the cross-country starts, not after.

ABOVE THE CABIN THE MARKERS ARE OCCASIONAL BLAZES ON TREES rather than tread. Blazes that stop appearing mean you have drifted; the slide alder will let you keep going anyway, which is why this is worth checking rather than assuming.

THE CAMP IS THE LAKE BASIN AT ABOUT 6,763 FT, and from it the route to this peak's south-west side goes up and over toward the col between it and its neighbour to the north-west.

BE CLEAR WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ON WHEN YOU ARRIVE. From this side the natural line gains the col at about 7,380 ft between the two peaks, which is where the glacier route on the north side starts. THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE INSTEAD WANTS THE TOE OF THE SOUTH-WEST GLACIER, WHICH IS REACHED BY TRAVERSING INTO OPEN HEATHER AND MORAINE BASINS ROUND THE TOE OF A ROCK BUTTRESS, NOT BY GAINING A COL. If you find yourself standing in a saddle between two summits, you are on the other route's start.
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the cabin
a long carry to a high camp
crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide
a camp position that makes descriptions written from the other approach misleading

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier._why: This route starts at a col rather than on a face, and the two camps that reach it sit on opposite sides of the mountain in different countries.
_sources: sibling row wa_mount_spickard_southwest for the Depot Creek detail

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
approach_variants.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A COL, NOT ON A FACE, AND THE COL IS BETWEEN TWO PEAKS. From the lake basin camp, gain the WIDE GULLY ON THE NORTH SIDE OF THE SADDLE and climb it to the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. The glacier route begins there.

RECOGNISE THE COL BY WHAT IS ON BOTH SIDES OF IT. You should be standing in a gap with a summit rising to either hand and ground falling away in front and behind. IF THE MOUNTAIN IS ABOVE YOU AND THERE IS NOTHING BEHIND YOU BUT THE SLOPE YOU CAME UP, YOU ARE ON A SHOULDER RATHER THAN THE COL.

THE GULLY IS THE POSITIVE MARKER ON THE WAY UP - a wide one, on the NORTH side of the saddle. A narrow gully, or one on the south side, is a different line.

AND THE NEGATIVE MARKER THAT MATTERS MOST: THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE ON THIS PEAK STARTS AT THE TOE OF A DIFFERENT GLACIER ON THE OTHER FLANK, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin
crevasses on the glacier above the col
a wide gully that collects anything falling from the slopes above it
a high camp with a long committing retreat

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
approach_variants.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE DEPOT CREEK CAMP YOU ARE APPROACHING THE COL FROM THE OPPOSITE SIDE, so descriptions written from the other camp will have the gully and the col in the wrong relative positions - read the ground rather than the page.

THE FIXED POINT IS THE SAME: THE COL AT ABOUT 7,380 FT BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS NEIGHBOUR TO THE NORTH-WEST. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully on the col's north side is the connection to the basin on the far side.

THE TEST THAT YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT GAP is that BOTH summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

DO NOT CONFUSE THIS START WITH THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME CAMP. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. IF YOU HAVE NOT GAINED A COL, YOU ARE NOT ON THIS ROUTE.
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at the falls
an overgrown approach road that washes out
crevasses on the ice above the col
two routes leaving one camp, with the wrong turn costing a day

wa_southeast_mox_peak_se_rib._why: There are two Mox summits side by side and the col between them is where parties commit to the wrong one; the approach is also long enough that the camp choice changes the shape of summit day.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
approach_variants.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS IS THE WHOLE NAVIGATION, AND THE TRAP IS THAT THERE ARE TWO SUMMITS.
