From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

AT THE COL, CHECK WHICH TOWER YOU ARE UNDER. THIS ROUTE IS ON THE EASTERN SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE HARDER AND HIGHER OF THE PAIR. IF THE PEAK ABOVE YOU IS THE ONE YOU TRAVERSED BENEATH ON THE WAY IN, YOU ARE FACING THE WESTERN SUMMIT AND HAVE TURNED THE WRONG WAY OUT OF THE SADDLE.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE THE COL IS A LADDER OF SPECIFIC SHAPES, IN ORDER, AND IT IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE RIGHT: a ramp leading RIGHT past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief DESCENT to a small flat area. THE FLAT SPOT AFTER A DOWNCLIMB IS THE CONFIRMATION - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

FROM THAT FLAT AREA, LOCATE THE CORRECT GULLY LEADING TO A HIGH NOTCH ON THE WEST RIDGE. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. IF YOU ARE UNCOILING A ROPE AT THE COL ITSELF, YOU ARE HUNDREDS OF FEET TOO LOW.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
approach_variants.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM EITHER CAMP THE ROUTE MEETS AT THE SAME PLACE: THE SADDLE BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

THE HIGH CAMP'S OWN MARKER IS THAT IT SITS ON ROCK OUTCROPS AT THE GLACIER'S EDGE at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

AT THE SADDLE, THE SUMMIT YOU WANT IS THE EASTERN ONE - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

THE CONFIRMATION SEQUENCE IS THE SAME LADDER: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short DOWNCLIMB to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin

wa_the_devils_club._why: This face is approached from the opposite side of the range from every other route on the peak, and the choice of which bank of the creek to travel is the approach's only real decision.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake to the Little Beaver landing, then the Perry Creek drainage
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn; the creek travel is the governing factor rather than the climbing
approach_variants.notes:
Access starts on the water. From the trailhead near milepost 134 walk down to the resort and take its water taxi, or paddle, a long way up the lake to the dock at its northern end. From the dock follow the maintained but lightly travelled valley trail west, through cedar and fir with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, to a camp with a three-sided log shelter - the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward this massif.

Beyond the shelter there is no trail. This is a genuinely serious approach and not a formality: the first ascent party spent two days and roughly fourteen hours of actual travel in the rain covering under two miles from the lake to the base, and described it as one of the worst approaches in the range. Expect cold fords, soaked gear, and skin torn by devil's club and slide alder - the plant the route is named for. Water is everywhere and should be treated.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHELTER IS THE LAST FIXED OBJECT YOU WILL SEE - a three-sided log structure at the camp. Everything after it is read off the creek.

STAY IN OR BESIDE THE CREEKBED ITSELF AS LONG AS IT LETS YOU. Rock-hopping and easy scrambling in the bed is the fastest travel available and it holds to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the channel and forces you up a bank.

THE ONE DECISION OF THE APPROACH IS WHICH BANK, AND IT HAS A RIGHT ANSWER: TAKE THE SOUTH, TRUE-LEFT SIDE. It holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths. THE NORTH SIDE IS A NEARLY IMPENETRABLE SLIDE-ALDER THICKET - so if you are swimming through continuous alder with no let-up and no open timber, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG BANK and the fix is to cross rather than to keep pushing.

THE CONFIRMATION THAT YOU CHOSE RIGHT COMES AS A CHANGE OF VEGETATION: above the alder band the forest opens into blueberry meadows and sparser timber, and travel speed roughly triples. If your speed has not changed, you have not cleared the band.

THE BASE IS THE CIRQUE AT THE HEAD OF THE DRAINAGE, beneath the connecting ridge that runs to the summit, with talus and season-dependent snowfields and moats guarding the toe of the face. THE FACE ITSELF IS THE FEATURE - a continuous wall of well over two thousand feet rising straight out of the cirque. IF THE GROUND ABOVE YOU IS BROKEN INTO LEDGES AND GULLIES RATHER THAN A SINGLE SUSTAINED FACE, YOU ARE UNDER THE FLANKING GROUND AND NOT UNDER THE ROUTE.

WATCH THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK AT THE TOE; how bad it is depends entirely on the season and it decides where the first pitch can start.
hazards: a water taxi or a paddle up a long lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
cold creek fords and continuously wet travel
devil's club and slide alder dense enough to stop progress on the wrong bank
avalanche paths on the north side of the drainage
moats between snowfield and rock at the toe of the face
a base days from any road with a very long retreat

wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier._why: The approach is the crux of this peak rather than the climbing, and the party's real choice is where to camp before a long roped crossing with almost no visual reference points on it.
_sources: web corroboration of the Colonial Glacier and col sequence

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
approach_variants.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CAMP IS FOUND BY REFUSING A SUMMIT. The climbers' path leads toward Pyramid Peak and the correct move is to drop slightly BEFORE it and traverse across scree and boulders to the moraine. IF YOU HAVE SCRAMBLED TO A SUMMIT, YOU HAVE CLIMBED THE WRONG PEAK AND GONE PAST THE TRAVERSE. The arrival marker is a meltwater tarn sitting against a terminal moraine with the ice above it.

FROM CAMP THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF THREE PIECES OF GROUND AND THEY MUST COME IN ORDER. First, rope up before leaving camp and climb the Colonial Glacier south past a rock feature on its east flank, on snow up to about thirty degrees, working around the moraine lake to a broad col near 6,840 ft. A STREAM RUNS AT THAT COL - a saddle with no water on it is not the right one.

Second, from the col you DROP roughly 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped. IF YOU ARE STILL GAINING HEIGHT AFTER THE COL, YOU HAVE NOT FOUND THE CROSSING. This is the stretch with no reference points, so track your line for the return; whiteout navigation here is the standing problem of the route.

Third, leave the glacier on the peak's NORTH-WEST side near a prominent rock feature around 7,700 ft and gain the west ridge by a class 3 gully with one exposed rib crossing. That puts you three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit. IF YOU ARE STILL ON ICE WITH THE SUMMIT PYRAMID RISING STRAIGHT ABOVE YOU AND NO GULLY BESIDE IT, YOU HAVE CROSSED TOO FAR AND ARE UNDER THE FACE RATHER THAN THE RIDGE.

The finish is a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, then a short exposed traverse onto the south side and blocky scrambling. You downclimb that notch on the way out, so read it as you pass.
hazards: a steep brushy unmaintained climbers' path with loose rock on the ridge crest
no water between the lake and the moraine tarn
crevasses on both glaciers, with bridges softening through the afternoon
a long crossing with almost no visual reference points, and whiteout navigation as the standing problem
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the west ridge
verglas or rime on the upper rock early in the season

approach_variants.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
approach_variants.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
approach_variants.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS IDENTIFIED BY THREE THINGS AT ONCE: it is broad, it has a stream on it, and the ground beyond it DROPS onto a second, much larger glacier. A saddle that is dry, or one with nothing but rock beyond it, is not this col.

FROM CAMP THE FIRST MOVE IS DOWNHILL - 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve - and then a roped crossing on which the cleanest line runs through the centre of the crevasse field. Bridges are usually sound by midsummer and need active route-finding around open slots. MARK YOUR OUTBOUND LINE. Coming back to a col you cannot see, across ground with no features, is the part of this route that goes wrong.

LEAVE THE ICE ON THE PEAK'S NORTH-WEST SIDE around 7,700 ft, near the prominent rock feature there, and take the class 3 gully with its single exposed rib crossing onto the west ridge, three to four hundred feet below the summit. IF THERE IS NO GULLY WHERE YOU STEP OFF THE ICE, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR ACROSS.
hazards: an exposed saddle camp with weather funnelling through it
a roped carry with overnight loads over crevassed ice
a featureless crossing that is committing in poor visibility from a high camp
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the ridge

wa_neve_glacier_west_ridge._why: Same approach as the standard line, and the whole difference is where you step off the ice - which is a decision made in the middle of a featureless glacier.
_sources: sibling row wa_snowfield_peak_neve_glacier for the detailed sequence

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead at about 1,150 ft on the highway, the maintained trail runs a little over two miles and fifteen hundred feet to the lake, where camping is prohibited. Continue on the rougher climbers' path along the lake's west side, which climbs steeply and directly - and with no water beyond this point - through talus and brush onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge and treeline camps near 5,400 ft. From there continue south to the terminal moraine of the Colonial Glacier, or to the col beyond it between about 6,000 and 6,800 ft, which is the usual base camp. The approach rather than the climbing is the crux of this route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WEST RIDGE IS GAINED FROM THE GLACIER BY A GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS THE POSITIVE MARKER. From camp, climb the Colonial Glacier to the broad col near 6,840 ft - it carries a stream, so a dry saddle is the wrong one - then drop 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve and cross it roped.

LEAVE THE ICE ON THE PEAK'S NORTH-WEST SIDE, near the prominent rock feature there around 7,700 ft. THE ENTRY IS A CLASS 3 GULLY WITH ONE EXPOSED RIB CROSSING IN IT, and it tops out on the ridge three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ON A GLACIER WITH NO LANDMARKS: IF YOU STEP OFF THE ICE ONTO ROCK THAT RISES STRAIGHT INTO THE SUMMIT PYRAMID WITH NO GULLY BESIDE IT, YOU HAVE CROSSED TOO FAR AND ARE UNDER THE FACE. Traverse back rather than committing upward - the face and the ridge are different propositions and the ridge is the easier ground.

THE SECOND CHECK IS THAT THE RIDGE HAS AIR ON BOTH SIDES. Once out of the gully you should be on a crest, not on a flank. A line that keeps a wall on one hand the whole way is not the ridge.

Above that the finish is common to both lines: a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, a short exposed traverse onto the south side, and blocky scrambling with one move that can feel low class 4. That notch is downclimbed on the exit, so read it on the way past.
hazards: a steep brushy climbers' path with no water above the lake
loose rock and short route-finding steps on the Pyramid east ridge crest
crevasses on the Colonial and Neve glaciers
a featureless crossing where the exit point must be identified by the gully rather than by position
one exposed rib crossing in the entry gully
an exposed notch traverse near the summit, reversed on the way down

wa_raven_ridge_standard_route._why: Two drainages on the same side of the range lead to two different points on one long ridge, and the ridge carries a second, lower summit that parties top out on by mistake.
_sources: web corroboration of the loose gully above the lake and the neighbouring lower point west of the saddle

approach_variants.name: Libby Creek road and Trail #415 to Libby Lake
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, after the snow has left the gully and before it returns to it
approach_variants.notes:
From the highway south-east of Twisp, turn up the Libby Creek road and follow the forest road system - a turn onto the main forest road, then a left, then a right onto a spur, then a left onto a second spur - to the small trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft. Roadside parking takes roughly ten vehicles and there is no toilet and no water.

Trail #415 climbs from there to Libby Lake. Watch for root holes and trail damage through the burned section in the lower and middle miles, which is uneven underfoot rather than hard to follow. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail high up and is used by some parties as a base camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY ABOVE THE LAKE IS THE ROUTE AND IT IS THE WORST GROUND OF THE DAY - that is how you know you are on it. From the lake basin, the line ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge crest. Parties routinely exit the gully about half-way up onto the RIB THAT PARALLELS IT, because the rib holds more solid rock; the rib is an escape from the gully rather than an alternative to it, so if you cannot see the gully from the rib you have wandered.

IF THE GROUND YOU ARE CLIMBING IS PLEASANT, YOU ARE NOT IN THE RIGHT GULLY. Several chutes rise out of this basin; the one that is the route is the one that leads to the saddle on the crest.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS ON THE RIDGE, NOT ON THE APPROACH: A SMALL PEAK STANDS JUST WEST OF THE SADDLE, AND IT IS NOT THE SUMMIT. Once on the crest the true high point is reached by an easy scramble EASTWARD along the ridge. IF YOU TOPPED OUT OF THE GULLY AND WENT LEFT TO A SUMMIT WITHIN A FEW MINUTES, YOU ARE ON THE LOWER POINT WEST OF THE SADDLE.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE TOP IS THE WALK. The true summit is a ridge scramble away over talus and large boulders, with intervening bumps, rather than an immediate high point above the gully. Ground you can traverse in minutes is the wrong answer here.

Also note the name trap in the roads and lakes on this side of the range: the drainage this variant uses and the one the south-east ridge uses have similarly named creeks and lakes on the same forest road system, so navigate by the road numbers and the trailhead you actually parked at rather than by the name of a lake.
hazards: an extremely loose gully that is the defining hazard of the route
rockfall from parties above in a confined chute
burned-out trail with root holes underfoot in the lower miles
no water or facilities at the trailhead
loose talus and large boulders on the ridge traverse
a lower summit west of the saddle that is easily mistaken for the top

approach_variants.name: From the Crater Creek road and the lake basin, gaining the crest from the south-east
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
approach_variants.notes:
The same summit is reached from the next drainage south. From the highway, take the Gold Creek road system on to forest road 4340 and then the Crater Creek spur to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft, where a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs a little under four miles to the lake, and from there the route continues off-trail up the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft.

This avoids the loose gully entirely at the price of more off-trail ridge travel, so it is the better option for a party unhappy with a confined chute and the worse one for a party short of time.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL ENDS AT THE LAKE AND THE RIDGE ABOVE IT BEGINS. The south-east ridge rises from the lake basin toward a col at about 8,000 ft - the ridge is the handrail and it should have ground falling away on both sides once you are established on it.

IF YOU FIND YOURSELF IN A CONFINED, VERY LOOSE CHUTE, YOU HAVE DROPPED OFF THE CREST INTO ONE OF THE GULLIES ON ITS FLANK. That is the other route's ground, approached from the other drainage, and it is not where this line goes.

AT THE COL, THE SUMMIT IS THE HIGH POINT ALONG THE CREST AND IT IS NOT THE FIRST BUMP. The ridge here carries several intervening high points, and a small peak stands west of the ridge saddle that is regularly mistaken for the top. THE TRUE SUMMIT IS THE EASTERN HIGH POINT; if you have gone west from a saddle and arrived quickly, you are on the wrong one.

The practical cross-check is talus. Reaching the true summit involves a tedious out-and-back over talus and large boulders rather than a quick step up from wherever you gained the crest.
hazards: a long off-trail ridge with no tread and no water above the lake
loose talus and large boulders on the crest
flanking gullies that will pull a party off the ridge into very loose ground
a day-use fee area with a long forest road drive
intervening high points that hide the true summit

wa_raven_ridge_southeast_ridge_crater_la._why: It shares a summit with the standard route but reaches it from a different drainage on a different forest road, and the two are easy to confuse because the lake names on this side of the range repeat.

approach_variants.name: Gold Creek and the Crater Creek spur to the lake, then the south-east ridge
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the upper ridge is out of snow
approach_variants.notes:
From Twisp, run south on the highway to the Gold Creek loop and continue onto the Gold Creek road, which becomes forest road 4340 after several miles. Turn onto the Crater Creek spur and follow it a little under five miles to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft; a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs just under four miles and roughly two thousand two hundred feet to the lake. From the lake the route leaves the trail and follows the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft and on to the summit.

Be careful with names when planning this one: the lake and creek names in this part of the range repeat across neighbouring drainages, and there is an unrelated lake and mountain of the same name in a different part of the state entirely. Navigate by the road numbers you turned onto and the trailhead elevation you actually parked at.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE LEAVES THE TRAIL AT THE LAKE - THERE IS NO TREAD BEYOND IT. From the lake basin the south-east ridge rises to the north-west toward a col at about 8,000 ft. THE RIDGE IS THE ROUTE AND THE TEST IS SYMMETRY: once established you should have ground falling away on both sides of you.

IF THE GROUND CLOSES IN AND YOU ARE CLIMBING A CONFINED, EXTREMELY LOOSE CHUTE, YOU HAVE SLIPPED OFF THE CREST ONTO A FLANKING GULLY. Those gullies are the other route's ground, gained from the next drainage north, and they are notably worse rock than the crest.

AT THE COL NEAR 8,000 FT THE SUMMIT IS ALONG THE CREST, NOT DIRECTLY ABOVE. A SMALL SEPARATE PEAK STANDS WEST OF THE RIDGE SADDLE AND IS ROUTINELY MISTAKEN FOR THE TOP; the true high point is the EASTERN one and reaching it is a tedious traverse over talus and large boulders past several intervening bumps.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS EFFORT, NOT ELEVATION: if you arrived at a summit within a few minutes of gaining the crest and did not cross bouldery bumps to get there, you are on the wrong high point and should look east along the ridge.
hazards: no water and no tread above the lake
loose talus and boulder-hopping along the crest
flanking gullies with very poor rock that will draw a party off the ridge
a long forest road drive on a fee trailhead
several false summits between the col and the true high point

approach_variants.name: From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415, gaining the crest by the gully above the lake
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the gully is free of snow
approach_variants.notes:
The other drainage reaches the same crest. From the Libby Creek road system - a turn onto the main forest road, a left, a right onto a spur and a left onto a second spur - park at the small roadside trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft, with no toilet and no water. Trail #415 leads to the lake, past a dilapidated cabin used by some parties as a camp, with root holes and burn damage underfoot in the lower and middle miles.

This approach is shorter to the crest and pays for it with a single very loose gully, which is the crux of that side of the mountain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LAKE THE CREST IS GAINED BY A LOOSE GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS UNPLEASANT ENOUGH THAT ITS QUALITY IS THE CONFIRMATION. Parties commonly exit it about half-way up onto the parallel rib, which holds more solid rock, and return to it higher; the rib is a refuge beside the gully rather than a separate line, so keep the gully in sight.

IF THE CHUTE YOU ARE IN IS SOLID AND ENJOYABLE, IT IS PROBABLY NOT THE ONE - several chutes rise out of this basin and the route's own is notorious.

AT THE TOP THE SADDLE IS ON THE CREST, AND THE SUMMIT IS EAST OF IT. A SMALL PEAK STANDS JUST WEST OF THE SADDLE; a summit reached in a few minutes by turning left out of the gully is that lower point, not the top.

THE TRUE HIGH POINT COSTS A TRAVERSE over talus and large boulders past intervening bumps. Arriving without that traverse means you are in the wrong place. Coming from this side the ridge is joined further west than the south-east ridge joins it, which is exactly why this mistake is easier to make on this approach than on the other one.
hazards: a very loose gully as the only way from the lake to the crest
rockfall onto a party strung out in a confined chute
burn damage and root holes on the lower trail
no water or facilities at the trailhead
the lower peak west of the saddle, which is easiest to mistake for the summit from this side

wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route._why: The peak stands within a mile of a much better known neighbour on the same crest, and the route is entered from a col on the far side of two glaciers - so knowing which col is the whole problem.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the overgrown section is passable and the creek has dropped
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at about 1,450 ft on the river road, Trail #768 runs six and a half miles - easy, well graded, mostly flat forest walking with a suspension bridge crossing - to a camp at about 2,440 ft. The maintained trail ends there.

Continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first and fording to the south side around 3,700 ft; treat that as a real crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large old avalanche-debris zone, and this stretch is slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber even in good conditions. Above the debris the path climbs to a pass near 5,900 ft, then drops about five hundred feet to a lake at about 5,338 ft. Most parties push on from there onto the ridge above at roughly 6,400 to 6,900 ft for high camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS ENTERED AT A COL, AND THERE ARE TWO COLS IN A ROW - GETTING THE ORDER RIGHT IS THE NAVIGATION. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the first glacier. Rope up before stepping onto the snow. Cross OVER the first col, then DESCEND the second, larger glacier to about 7,200 ft, then TRAVERSE RIGHT - eastward - across it.

THE COL YOU WANT IS AT ABOUT 7,640 FT AND IT SITS BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS LARGER NEIGHBOUR TO THE WEST. A BERGSCHRUND GUARDS IT and can be hard to cross late in the season, sometimes needing a short rappel to get down onto or across it. THE SCHRUND IS THE CONFIRMATION AS MUCH AS THE OBSTACLE: a col reached without one is likely the first col, not the second.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE COL IS WHERE YOU GO NEXT: CONTOUR ON AN EASY SNOWFIELD ROUND TO THE PEAK'S SOUTH SIDE and climb a loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge. IF YOU ARE STILL ON THE NORTH OR SHADED SIDE OF THE CREST WITH THE FACE ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE NOT CONTOURED FAR ENOUGH ROUND.

THE MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT WHICH MOUNTAIN YOU ARE ON. THE SUMMIT LIES JUST UNDER A MILE EAST OF ITS BETTER-KNOWN NEIGHBOUR ALONG THE CONNECTING RIDGE. If you have topped out on the summit block immediately above the first col you crossed, you are on the neighbour, not on this peak. Keep going east.

There is also a direct alternative from the col: an exposed class 3+ ridge taken straight from the saddle instead of the gully. Both finish on the same crest; the gully is the standard and the loose rock in it is the main hazard on the climb.
hazards: a real creek ford at about 3,700 ft, dangerous in high water
an old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber
crevasses on both glaciers, with rope and rescue gear required
a bergschrund at the col that has needed a short rappel late in the season
very loose rock in the gully to the west ridge
a multi-day committing position with a long retreat

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ridge camp is exposed to weather in a way the lake is not
approach_variants.notes:
The lake at about 5,338 ft is reached by dropping five hundred feet off the pass and has reliable water and good camping. The ridge above it, between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft, is the higher camp most parties use, with open views across to the peaks and a much shorter summit day. The trade is exposure and a further climb at the end of an already long day in.

The drop from the pass into the lake basin holds snow into midsummer, and on snow it is normally the crux navigation of the approach day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
EITHER CAMP FEEDS THE SAME LINE: TRAVERSE THE UPPER BASINS NEAR 7,000 FT TO GAIN THE FIRST GLACIER, CROSS ITS COL, DESCEND THE SECOND GLACIER TO ABOUT 7,200 FT, AND TRAVERSE EAST TO THE 7,640 FT COL BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS NEIGHBOUR.

COUNT THE COLS. The first is crossed and the second is the destination, with a bergschrund on it. Standing at a col with a large icefield behind you and the summit block immediately above is the FIRST col and the neighbouring peak, not this one.

FROM THE CORRECT COL, CONTOUR ROUND ON EASY SNOW TO THE PEAK'S SOUTH SIDE AND FIND THE LOOSE GULLY. A route that climbs directly out of the col on exposed class 3+ crest is the direct variant rather than the standard, so choose it deliberately rather than by accident.

If you camped at the lake, budget the extra height gain into the morning; if you camped on the ridge, budget the wind into the night.
hazards: a five-hundred-foot descent into the lake basin, on snow into midsummer
an exposed ridge camp
crevassed glaciers between camp and the col
a bergschrund guarding the col
no easy retreat once past the first col

wa_sinister_peak_north_face._why: It shares the whole multi-day approach with the standard route and then deliberately does not stop at the col that route uses - and a party that turns uphill too early ends up on the other side of the mountain.
_sources: sibling row wa_sinister_peak_southwest_route for the shared approach detail

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
approach_variants.season: Late July through September for the approach; the face itself favours a firm, cold night
approach_variants.notes:
The walk-in is the standard route's: Trail #768 six and a half miles to the camp at about 2,440 ft, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, a ford to the south side near 3,700 ft, the old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber, a pass near 5,900 ft, a lake at about 5,338 ft, and a high camp on the ridge above between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft.

From camp the difference begins: continue over the col between the two glaciers at about 8,500 ft and descend onto the larger northern icefield, then traverse beneath the peak's north side to reach the foot of the face.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEFINING INSTRUCTION IS THAT YOU DO NOT TURN UPHILL AT THE COL THE STANDARD ROUTE USES. From the glacier col, descend onto the big icefield and KEEP TRAVERSING EAST BENEATH THE PEAK. The base of this route is out on that ice, under the face, not at any saddle.

IF YOU HAVE CLIMBED TO A COL WITH A BERGSCHRUND ON IT AND ARE LOOKING AT AN EASY SNOWFIELD CONTOURING ROUND TO A SUNNY SIDE, YOU HAVE ARRIVED AT THE STANDARD ROUTE'S ENTRY AT ABOUT 7,640 FT AND GONE PAST YOUR OWN. Drop back onto the ice and continue east under the wall.

THE ASPECT IS THE OTHER TEST AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS. This face is the SHADED side. If the wall above you is in morning or afternoon sun while the icefield behind you is bright, you are round on the southern flank and looking at the wrong ground. The face should be holding shadow when the rest of the basin is not.

AND CHECK THE MOUNTAIN, NOT JUST THE FACE. This summit sits just under a mile EAST of its larger and better-known neighbour along the connecting crest, and the same icefield runs beneath both. A north face reached quickly after crossing the first col is the neighbour's; keep traversing until the summit above you is the eastern one.

Watch the bergschrund at the foot of the face, which is a separate feature from the one on the standard route's col and behaves differently through the season.
hazards: the same ford, avalanche-debris zone and brushy climbers' path as the standard approach
a descent onto a large crevassed icefield with the return climb still to come
a long traverse beneath a face, exposed to anything coming off it
a bergschrund at the base of the face
a shaded north aspect that holds hard ice and cold, with a committing position
an approach that reaches its base by losing height, so retreat means re-climbing

approach_variants.name: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn, and only as part of a larger traverse of the range
approach_variants.notes: The first ascent came at the face from the other direction, from the col to the west, traversing the northern icefield across to the peak. That is the natural line for a party already high in this range on a multi-peak traverse rather than for a party walking in for this route alone; it involves no new trailhead but a great deal more glacier travel, and it should be planned as one leg of a bigger trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVING FROM THE WEST, THE ICEFIELD IS THE HIGHWAY AND THE PEAK IS PICKED OFF IT. Traverse east along the ice beneath the crest until the summit above you is the EASTERN of the two on this section of ridge - the larger, better-known peak lies just under a mile to the west, so the first big north face you pass is not yours.

THE FACE IS THE SHADED ONE. If the wall you are approaching takes direct sun while the ice around you is in shadow, you are on the wrong aspect or the wrong peak.

THE BASE IS ON THE ICE ITSELF, BENEATH THE WALL, with a bergschrund at the junction. THERE IS NO COL INVOLVED - if you have climbed to a saddle to reach your start, you have joined the standard route's entry on the far side of the crest instead.

Because this arrival involves no fixed camp of its own, fix a retreat plan before crossing beneath the face: the ground you traverse in to reach it is the ground you must reverse to leave, and it is all crevassed.
hazards: long committed glacier travel with no camp of its own
crevasses across the whole traverse
exposure beneath a face for the length of the approach
a bergschrund at the foot of the wall
a plan that only makes sense inside a larger traverse, so a retreat is a multi-day proposition

wa_snowking_mountain_standard._why: The approach opens with a road walk and then depends on spotting one unsigned path leaving it, which is far harder to find from above on the way out than from below on the way in.
_sources: web corroboration of the road walk and the ribbon-marked climbers' path

approach_variants.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
approach_variants.season: June through September
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HARDEST THING TO FIND ON THIS APPROACH IS THE PATH ITSELF, AND IT IS FOUND AT A FIREPIT. Walk the closed roadbed uphill through windfall and encroaching brush, crossing two large washouts, until the road ENDS at a small clearing with an old firepit. THE CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES ON THE LEFT NEAR THAT CLEARING, unsigned and steep from its first step. FIX THE SPOT IN YOUR MIND ON THE WAY IN - from above, in fog, it is much harder to find, and parties overshoot it on the descent.

THE SECOND DECISION IS A CAIRNED FORK NEAR 5,200 FT. A fainter fisherman's trail drops away toward a lake; STAY RIGHT AND UPHILL ON THE CLIMBERS' PATH. IF YOU ARE LOSING HEIGHT TOWARD WATER, YOU HAVE TAKEN THE FISHERMAN'S TRAIL.

EXPECT TO LOSE THE TREAD ON THE RIDGE AND NOT TO PANIC ABOUT IT. Through grass and boulders the path is faint and parties routinely lose it and pick it up again a few hundred feet higher. WHEN IN DOUBT, STAY ON THE CREST.

THE CLIMB PROPER STARTS ABOVE THE LAKE MEADOWS. Work round the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A ROCK WALL LINES THE EAST SIDE OF THAT OUTLET; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the END of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall itself. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west onto slabs and benches, past small tarns, then traverse rocky slopes to a notch and take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier.

ROPE UP BEFORE STEPPING ONTO THE SNOW, NOT PART-WAY ACROSS. IF YOU ARE TRYING TO CLIMB A ROCK WALL BESIDE THE OUTLET STREAM, YOU HAVE MISSED THE TURN AROUND ITS END.
hazards: an unsigned path leaving the roadbed that is easy to miss on the descent, especially in fog
two large washouts on the road walk, awkward in high snowmelt
no water between the road and the boggy bench near 4,800 ft
a faint ridge tread through grass and boulders that is routinely lost
crevasses and exposed blue ice on the glacier by mid to late summer
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
approach_variants.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER CAMP YOU USE, THE CLIMB STARTS AT THE HEAD OF THE LAKE'S OUTLET STREAM. Work counterclockwise round the lake to the outlet. A ROCK WALL RUNS ALONG THE EAST SIDE OF IT - the move is to drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the END of that wall with a single class 3 step. FORCING THE WALL DIRECTLY IS THE WRONG ANSWER AND IS HOW PARTIES GET STOPPED HERE.

Above the wall, climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto slabs and benches. Past the small tarns, traverse rocky slopes toward the notch and take the short drop into the gap onto the glacier.

THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE NOTCH, NOT THE ANGLE. You should step DOWN into a gap to reach the ice. If you have walked onto snow without dropping through a notch, you are on a different bench and should keep traversing.

Cross the glacier to the south-west aiming straight at the peak and leave the snow for rock on the LEFT, where a faint scree path picks up. Sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks finishes it from the south-east ridge or the south slope.
hazards: wind-exposed benches with limited flat ground
seasonal water at the low bench that can dry to puddles
cliff bands on the buttress that must be turned rather than climbed
a crevassed stretch of glacier below the notch
timing the return before the afternoon softens the bridges

wa_east_ridge_2._why: It shares the first mile with the standard route and then turns the opposite way at a junction the row describes as easy to miss - which is exactly the kind of fork that costs a party a day.

approach_variants.name: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
approach_variants.season: June through September
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles to the signed forest road 1570 junction and turn right. Cross the river on a concrete bridge and continue about half a mile to a Y-junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders; park there, at roughly 1,150 to 1,300 ft, because a long-standing washout keeps most parties from driving higher.

A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every fifty to a hundred and fifty feet leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth - about seventeen hundred vertical feet in its first mile, with few switchbacks - to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. From the saddle the route climbs roughly a thousand feet to Peak 5791, then traverses heather benches and meadows above the lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of the east ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE JUNCTION AT THE SADDLE IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS APPROACH AND IT IS EASY TO MISS. At the ridge saddle near Point 5116, GO LEFT and climb about a thousand feet to Peak 5791. IF YOU FIND YOURSELF DROPPING TOWARD A LAKE, OR CONTOURING THE WEST SIDE OF THE CREST ON A FAINT TREAD, YOU HAVE TAKEN THE OTHER BRANCH AND ARE ON THE KINDY RIDGE LINE THAT SERVES THE STANDARD ROUTE.

THE PINK RIBBON IS THE HANDRAIL ON THE STEEP MILE BELOW. It is spaced closely enough that losing sight of it for long means you have drifted; the tread is rooty and eroded and very slick when wet, so on the descent the ribbon matters more than the ground does.

ABOVE THE SADDLE THE MARKERS ARE TWO NAMED HIGH POINTS IN ORDER: Peak 5791 first, then heather benches and meadows above the lake, then Peak 5860 crossed or contoured. YOU SHOULD PASS TWO DISTINCT POINTS BEFORE THE RIDGE BEGINS - arriving at what you take for the base without having crossed them means you are short.

THE BASE ITSELF IS WHERE THE EAST RIDGE RISES OUT OF THE GROUND ABOVE THE LAKE BASIN AND RUNS WEST TOWARD THE SUMMIT. IF THE GROUND AHEAD OF YOU IS A GLACIER RATHER THAN A RIDGE, YOU HAVE CONTOURED PAST THE RIDGE'S FOOT AND JOINED THE STANDARD ROUTE'S APPROACH TO THE ICE. The east ridge is rock and heather with air on both sides; the standard route crosses snow.

Note that the two routes on this peak describe the ridge junctions differently and one says go left where the other says stay right at a fork. They are not the same fork. Follow the description belonging to the route you intend to climb and use the physical markers - a ribbon-marked steep mile, a saddle, then two high points - rather than reconciling the two.
hazards: a rooty, eroded and very slick steep mile that is worse descending than ascending
an easy-to-miss junction at the saddle where the two routes on this peak diverge
no water on the steep climb from the roadbed
rolling ridge travel that takes longer than the distance suggests
an exposed camp and no bail-out once out on the ridge

approach_variants.name: Camping at the lake below the ridge
approach_variants.season: Same window
approach_variants.notes: The lake below the ridge is the common overnight for this route and turns it from a very long day into a comfortable two. The camping is in the meadows on the lake's east side and there is reliable water. Parties doing it in a day still pass through the same ground and should treat the lake as the last water before the ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LAKE THE BASE OF THE EAST RIDGE IS GAINED BY CROSSING OR CONTOURING PEAK 5860 AND CONTINUING ON HEATHER BENCHES ABOVE THE BASIN. The ridge foot is where that benched ground runs out against the crest and the rock begins rising west toward the summit.

THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE ON A CREST, NOT ON A BENCH. Once established the ground should fall away on both sides. Heather benches with a wall above you and the basin below are still the approach.

AND THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS SNOW. IF YOU ARE STEPPING ONTO GLACIER ICE, YOU HAVE CONTOURED ROUND PAST THE FOOT OF THE RIDGE AND ARE ON THE STANDARD ROUTE'S GROUND. Turn back and gain the crest.

Carry water from the lake. There is none on the ridge.
hazards: no water above the lake
a wind-exposed basin camp
loose blocks where the ridge rises out of the benches
committing ridge travel with no easy descent off either side

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir._why: The lake below the peak can be reached from two directions - a pass on the west or the valley on the east - and the row's own records disagree about the eastern one, so the western line is the one a party can actually follow.
_sources: sibling row wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes for the valley alternative

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
approach_variants.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COULOIR IS VISIBLE FROM THE LAKE AND THAT IS THE POINT OF APPROACHING FROM THIS SIDE. From the water, look south-west at the peak: THE ROUTE IS THE OBVIOUS NORTH-FACING SNOW LINE THAT SPLITS THE SUMMIT BLOCK ITSELF. Pick it out before you start moving, because from underneath the flanking gullies all look alike.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHERE THE LINE ENDS. IT MUST TOP OUT ON THE SUMMIT BLOCK, NOT ON THE RIDGE BESIDE IT. A couloir that finishes at a notch with more mountain above it and to one side is one of the flanking gullies and not the route.

THE SECOND TEST IS ASPECT. This is the NORTH side: it should be the shaded flank, holding firmer snow than anything around it in the morning and going soft late. IF THE SNOW YOU ARE STANDING ON IS IN EARLY SUN, YOU HAVE COME ROUND ONTO AN EASTERN OR WESTERN FLANK.

THE THIRD TEST IS CONTINUITY. The route is a single continuous line from the basin to the top of the block. If the snow you are following breaks into disconnected patches with rock steps between them, you are either too late in the season for it or on a different feature.

AND CHECK THE MOUNTAIN. There is a similarly named peak elsewhere in the range that is reached from an entirely different valley and has nothing to do with this one. The confirmation here is that the lake lies immediately north-east of your peak and the summit stands directly across it from you.
hazards: a corniced pass early in the season, with an alternative col that carries its own hazards
a descent east from the pass that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
avalanche terrain in the couloir and the basin below it in spring
wet-snow release and rockfall out of the couloir once the sun reaches the face
a remote basin with a long retreat and no trail on the eastern side

approach_variants.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
approach_variants.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIXED POINT ON THIS SIDE IS THE LAKE, AND EVERYTHING ABOVE IT IS READ OFF THE PEAK ITSELF. The lake sits immediately NORTH-EAST of the summit, so from the water the mountain stands to the south-west and the route faces you.

THE ROUTE IS THE CONTINUOUS NORTH-FACING SNOW LINE CLEAVING THE SUMMIT BLOCK. It must finish ON the block. A gully that tops out on the ridge to either side of the summit is a flanking line, not the route.

USE SHADE AS THE CONFIRMATION: the north side holds shadow while the basin around it is lit, and the snow in it stays firm longest in the morning.

BECAUSE THE APPROACH FROM THIS SIDE IS UNMARKED, FIX YOUR LINE INTO THE BASIN ON THE WAY IN. There is no tread to follow back out, and the basin has no obvious exit when seen from above.
hazards: an approach that depends on boat or floatplane schedules to reach the valley at all
an unmarked, steep off-trail push into the basin with no tread to follow out
conflicting written descriptions of which drainage is used, so navigate from maps rather than prose
avalanche terrain in the couloir in spring
a long committing distance from any road

wa_trapper_mountain_south_slopes._why: The peak's easy side is the far side from the road, and the row's own approach description and its own waypoints disagree about which drainage gets you there.
_sources: route row approach/waypoints columns (re-homed, with the internally contradicted drainage claim deliberately not repeated)
sibling row wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir for the pass approach

approach_variants.name: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn, once the basin is walkable and the valley road and trail are open
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

One caution about the paperwork rather than the ground: the written descriptions of this approach and the recorded waypoints for it name different drainages for that off-trail section, and the recorded distances do not match the recorded positions. Plan the departure point from current maps and imagery rather than from any single written description.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LAKE IS THE ANCHOR AND THE ROUTE IS READ FROM IT. The lake sits immediately NORTH-EAST of the summit, so from the water the peak is to the south-west.

LEAVE THE LAKE BASIN AND GAIN THE BROAD BASIN AND SLOPES DIRECTLY ABOVE IT ON THE SOUTH SIDE, aiming for the LOW POINT ON THE SUMMIT RIDGE rather than for the summit itself. There are no cairns and no path here; the terrain is the navigation.

THE GROUND CONFIRMS ITSELF AS YOU GAIN HEIGHT: loose unconsolidated talus interspersed with heather benches on a steep grade, with unstable footing and no established tread. NOTE YOUR ASCENT LINE, because on the descent one talus-and-heather slope looks exactly like the next and there is nothing to follow.

THE FINISH IS THE TEST THAT YOU CHOSE THE RIGHT SIDE. From the ridge the last stretch to the top is a short EXPOSED CLASS 3 SCRAMBLE. IF THE GROUND ABOVE YOU IS A STEEP CONTINUOUS SNOW LINE SPLITTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK, YOU HAVE COME ROUND ONTO THE NORTH SIDE AND ARE UNDER THE COULOIR ROUTE, which is a different proposition entirely and wants an axe, crampons and a season this route does not.

Also confirm the peak: a similarly named summit elsewhere in the range is approached from a completely different valley. The lake immediately north-east of your summit is what identifies this one.
hazards: reaching the valley at all depends on a ferry or floatplane and a shuttle
an unmarked off-trail push into the basin with no reliable path
loose unconsolidated talus and steep heather benches with unstable footing
no tread to follow on the descent, on ground where every slope looks the same
an exposed class 3 finish off the ridge
conflicting records of the approach drainage, so the departure point must be planned from maps

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west
approach_variants.season: Late spring into summer, while the pass is straightforward and the basin beyond is still simple travel
approach_variants.notes:
The lake can also be reached from the other side of the range, by climbing to the pass at about 5,392 ft at the head of the river road - or the nearby col used when the pass is corniced - and then travelling east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond to the lake at about 4,170 ft.

This avoids the ferry and the unmarked valley push entirely, at the cost of a pass crossing in each direction and a descent that has to be re-climbed at the end of the trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE PASS THE TRAVEL IS EAST AND DOWNHILL TO THE LAKE, so the arrival marker is water at about 4,170 ft with the peak standing to the SOUTH-WEST of it.

FROM THE LAKE, THE SOUTH SLOPES ARE GAINED BY GOING ROUND THE PEAK, NOT UP THE SIDE FACING YOU. The face you can see from the lake is the northern one. THE ROUTE IS ON THE OPPOSITE FLANK - the broad basin and slopes above the lake basin on the south side, taken toward the low point on the summit ridge.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SNOW LINE. IF YOU ARE LOOKING UP AT A CONTINUOUS COULOIR SPLITTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK AND ARE TEMPTED BY IT, THAT IS THE NORTH COULOIR ROUTE AND NOT THIS ONE. It is a snow climb with a different season and different equipment.

THE POSITIVE MARKERS ON THE ROUTE ARE UNDERFOOT: loose talus and heather benches on a steep grade, with no cairns, followed by an exposed class 3 scramble off the ridge to the top. Note your ascent line for the descent, because nothing here is marked.
hazards: a corniced pass in early season
a descent from the pass that must be re-climbed on the way out
loose talus and heather with unstable footing and no tread
an exposed class 3 finish
a basin with no path and no obvious exit seen from above

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face._why: Two trailheads reach the same pass by very different means, and beyond the pass the tower and the mountain sit on one ridge - so the choice of trailhead and the choice of formation are two separate ways to end up in the wrong place.
_sources: web corroboration of the two trailhead options and their relative gain

approach_variants.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
approach_variants.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,050 to 5,800 ft depending on which record you read.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE PASS IS THE GATE AND THE CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES DIRECTLY FROM THE TOP OF IT. Do not look for it below the pass or beyond it: an unmaintained path runs SOUTH along the ridge from the pass itself. IF YOU ARE CASTING ABOUT ON THE TRAIL BELOW THE PASS FOR A JUNCTION, YOU HAVE NOT GOT HIGH ENOUGH.

THE TOWER IS A DISTINCT ROCK TOWER ON THAT CREST AND IT IS THE FIRST ONE. The face you want looks back toward the pass on the NORTH-EAST side, so from the path it presents itself as you approach rather than after you have passed it.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOUNTAIN FURTHER ALONG THE SAME RIDGE. If you have walked past the tower and are looking at a broad peak with a lake basin below it, YOU HAVE CONTINUED TO THE MOUNTAIN AND GONE PAST THE TOWER. Turn round; the tower is a slender formation and the mountain is not.

THE ROUTE CONFIRMS ITSELF ON THE SECOND PITCH: two pitches of easy fifth class, with the upper one DIAGONALLING LEFT INTO A GULLY AND FINISHING AT A LARGE BOULDER NEAR THE TOP. A line that runs straight up with no leftward gully, or that takes more than a couple of pitches, is not this face.

One more caution about names: there are several mountains called Thunder in this state and more than one formation of this sort on crest trails. The identifying combination here is a pass on the long-distance crest trail with an unmaintained path leaving its top southward, and a tower standing before the mountain on the same ridge.
hazards: an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass with no signage
a long enough round trip that many parties camp, so a day attempt commits to a late finish
loose rock on the tower and on the ridge approach to it
a two-pitch face that still needs a rope, a rack and a plan to get back down
no water on the ridge between the pass and the tower

approach_variants.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
approach_variants.season: July through September
approach_variants.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE PASS THE APPROACH IS IDENTICAL TO THE OTHER TRAILHEAD'S: AN UNMAINTAINED CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES THE TOP OF THE PASS AND RUNS SOUTH ALONG THE RIDGE.

THE TOWER IS THE FIRST DISTINCT ROCK FORMATION ON THAT CREST, AND ITS NORTH-EAST FACE LOOKS BACK TOWARD THE PASS. Because this approach arrives at the pass from below and in trees, take a moment on the pass itself to pick the tower out along the crest before starting the path - it is much harder to identify from underneath.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SAME AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: THE MOUNTAIN LIES FURTHER ALONG THE SAME RIDGE, ABOVE A LAKE BASIN. A broad peak with lakes below it is not the tower. If you are walking under a mountainside rather than under a slender formation, you have gone too far.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB ITSELF: two pitches of easy fifth class with the second diagonalling LEFT into a gully to a large boulder near the top. If your first pitch is hard or your route runs straight up a face for several rope lengths, you are not on it.
hazards: more climbing than the other trailhead for a slightly shorter distance
forested trail the whole way, with little view of conditions ahead
an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass
loose rock on the tower
no water on the ridge beyond the pass
